Stable Boundary Spike Clusters for the Two-Dimensional Gierer-Meinhardt System

Weiwei Ao Address: Wuhan University, Department of Mathematics, China, 430072 Email address: wwao@whu.edu.cn , Juncheng Wei Address: Department of Mathematics, University of British Columbia, Vancouver, B.C., Canada, V6T 1Z2 Email address: jcwei@math.ubc.ca and Matthias Winter Address: Brunel University London, Department of Mathematics, Uxbridge UB8 3PH, United Kingdom Email address: matthias.winter@brunel.ac.uk
Abstract.

We consider the Gierer-Meinhardt system with small inhibitor diffusivity and very small activator diffusivity in a bounded and smooth two-dimensional domain. For any given positive integer kk we construct a spike cluster consisting of kk boundary spikes which all approach the same nondegenerate local maximum point of the boundary curvature. We show that this spike cluster is linearly stable.

The main idea underpinning these stable spike clusters is the following: due to the small inhibitor diffusivity the interaction between spikes is repulsive and the spikes are attracted towards a nondegenerate local maximum point of the boundary curvature. Combining these two effects can lead to an equilibrium of spike positions within the cluster such that the cluster is linearly stable.

Keywords: Pattern formation, reaction-diffusion system, spike, cluster, stability.

1. Introduction

Turing in his pioneering work in 1952 [14] proposed that a patterned distribution of two chemical substances, called the morphogens, could trigger the emergence of cell structures. He also gives the following explanation for the formation of the morphogenetic pattern: It is assumed that one of the morphogens, the activator, diffuses slowly and the other, the inhibitor, diffuses much faster. In the mathematical framework of a coupled system of reaction-diffusion equations with hugely different diffusion coefficients it is shown by linear stability analysis that the homogeneous state may be unstable. In particular, a small perturbation of spatially homogeneous initial data may evolve to a stable spatially complex pattern of the morphogens.

Since the work of Turing, many different reaction-diffusion system in biological modelling have been proposed and the occurrence of pattern formation has been investigated by studying what is now called Turing instability. One of the most popular models in biological pattern formation is the Gierer-Meinhardt system [5], see also [10]. In two dimensions in a special case after rescaling it can be stated as follows:

{ut=ε2Δu−u+u2v,u>0 in Ω,τvt=DΔv−v+u2,v>0 in Ω,∂u∂ν=∂v∂ν=0​ on ​∂Ω.\left\{\begin{array}[]{l}u_{t}=\varepsilon^{2}\Delta u-u+\frac{u^{2}}{v},u>0\mbox{ in }\Omega,\\[5.69054pt] \tau v_{t}=D\Delta v-v+u^{2},v>0\mbox{ in }\Omega,\\[5.69054pt] \frac{\partial u}{\partial\nu}=\frac{\partial v}{\partial\nu}=0\mbox{ on }\partial\Omega.\end{array}\right. (1.1)

The unknown functions u=u⁡(x,t)u=u(x,t) and v=v⁡(x,t)v=v(x,t) represent the concentrations of the activator and inhibitor, respectively, at the point x∈Ω⊂ℝ2x\in\Omega\subset{\mathbb{R}}^{2} and at a time t>0t>0. Here Δ\Delta is the Laplace operator in ℝ2{\mathbb{R}}^{2}, Ω\Omega is a smooth bounded domain in ℝ2{\mathbb{R}}^{2}, ν=ν⁡(x)\nu=\nu(x) is the outer unit normal at x∈∂Ωx\in\partial\Omega.

Throughout this paper, we assume that

0<ε≪1, 0<D≪1,0<\varepsilon\ll 1,\ 0<D\ll 1, (1.2)

τ≥0\tau\geq 0 is a fixed constant independent of ε\varepsilon, DD and xx. Further, the diffusivities ε\varepsilon and DD do not depend on xx but they are both small constants. In this paper, we further assume that

e−1D≪ε≪D.e^{-\frac{1}{\sqrt{D}}}\ll\varepsilon\ll\sqrt{D}. (1.3)

This means that ϵ\epsilon is much smaller than D{D}. On the other hand, ϵ\epsilon cannot be exponentially small compared to D\sqrt{D}.

In this paper, we study the Gierer-Meinhardt system in a bounded and smooth two-dimensional domain. We prove the existence and stability of a cluster consisting of kk boundary spikes near a nondegenerate local maximum point P0P^{0} of the boundary curvature h⁡(P)h(P).

The main idea underpinning these stable spike clusters is the following: due to the small inhibitor diffusivity the interaction between spikes is repulsive and the spikes are attracted towards a nondegenerate local maximum point of the boundary curvature. Combining these two effects can lead to an equilibrium of spike positions within the cluster such that the cluster is linearly stable.

The repulsive nature of spikes has been shown in [4]. Existence and stability of a spike cluster made up of two boundary spikes has been established in [3].

Before we state our main results, let us mention some previous ones concerning various regimes for the asymptotic behavior of DD.

For the strong coupling case, i.e. D∼1D\sim 1, the second and third authors constructed single-interior spike solutions [20]. In [22], they continued the study, and proved the existence of solutions with kk interior spikes.

Moreover, it is shown that this solution is linearly stable for τ=0\tau=0.

For the weak coupling case D→∞D\to\infty, in [21] the second and third authors proved the existence of multiple interior spike solutions. Further, they showed that there are stability thresholds

D1​(ε)>D2​(ε)>⋯>Dk​(ε)>⋯D_{1}(\varepsilon)>D_{2}(\varepsilon)>\cdots>D_{k}(\varepsilon)>\cdots

such that if limε→0Dk​(ε)D>1\lim_{\varepsilon\to 0}\frac{D_{k}(\varepsilon)}{D}>1, the kk-peak solution is stable and if limε→0Dk​(ε)D<1\lim_{\varepsilon\to 0}\frac{D_{k}(\varepsilon)}{D}<1, the kk-peak solution is unstable. Multiple spikes for the Gierer-Meinhardt system in a one-dimensional interval have been studied in [13, 7, 23] and on the real line in [2].

In [17] the existence, uniqueness and spectral properties of a boundary spike solution have been studied for the shadow Gierer-Meinhardt system (i.e. after formally taking the limit D→∞D\to\infty.)

In [24] the existence and stability of N−N-peaked steady states for the Gierer-Meinhardt system with precursor inhomogeneity has been explored. The spikes in the patterns can vary in amplitude. In particular, the results imply that a precursor inhomogeneity can induce instability. Single-spike solutions for the Gierer-Meinhardt system with precursor including spike dynamics have been studied in [15].

Previous results on stable spike clusters include a stable spike cluster for a consumer chain model [25] and a stable spike cluster for the one-dimensional Gierer-Meinhardt system with precursor inhomogeneity [27].

For more background, modelling, analysis and computation on the Gierer-Meinhardt system, we refer to [26] and the references therein.

2. Main Results: Existence and Stability

Let Ω⊂ℝ2\Omega\subset{\mathbb{R}}^{2} be bounded and smooth two-dimensional domain. Let ww be the unique solution in H1​(ℝ2)H^{1}({\mathbb{R}}^{2}) of the problem

{Δ​w−w+w2=0,w⁡(0)=maxy∈ℝ2⁡w⁡(y),w⁡(y)→0​ as |y|→∞.\left\{\begin{array}[]{l}\Delta w-w+w^{2}=0,\\[5.69054pt] w(0)=\max_{y\in{\mathbb{R}}^{2}}w(y),\ w(y)\to 0\mbox{ as }|y|\to\infty.\end{array}\right. (2.1)

For the existence and uniqueness of (2.1), we refer to [8] and [11]. We also recall that ww is radially symmetric and

w⁡(y)∼|y|−12​e−|y| as ​|y|→∞w(y)\sim|y|^{-\frac{1}{2}}e^{-|y|}\quad\mbox{ as }|y|\to\infty

and

w′​(y)=−(1+o⁡(1))​w​(y) as ​|y|→∞,w^{\prime}(y)=-(1+o(1))w(y)\quad\mbox{ as }|y|\to\infty,

where w′w^{\prime} is the radial derivative of ww, i.e. w′=wr​(r)w^{\prime}=w_{r}(r).

Theorem 2.1.

Let kk be a positive integer, and P0P^{0} be a nondegenerate local maximum point of the curvature h⁡(P)h(P) of the boundary ∂Ω\partial\Omega.

Then for 0<e−1D≪ε≪D≪10<e^{-\frac{1}{\sqrt{D}}}\ll\varepsilon\ll\sqrt{D}\ll 1, the Gierer-Meinhardt system (1.1) has a kk-boundary spike cluster steady-state solution (uϵ,vϵ)(u_{\epsilon},v_{\epsilon}) which concentrates near P0P^{0}. In particular, it satisfies

uϵ∼D​ξσϵ2​∑i=1kw⁡(x−Pi,ϵϵ),u_{\epsilon}\sim\frac{D\xi_{\sigma}}{\epsilon^{2}}\sum_{i=1}^{k}w(\frac{x-P_{i,\epsilon}}{\epsilon}),

where Pi,ϵ→P0P_{i,\epsilon}\to P^{0} as ϵ→0\epsilon\to 0 for i=1,2,…,ki=1,2,\ldots,k.

Further, we have

ξσ∼1log⁡Dϵ\xi_{\sigma}\sim\frac{1}{\log\frac{\sqrt{D}}{\epsilon}}

and

|Pi−Pi−1|∼Dlogξσϵ​D,i=2,…,k.|P_{i}-P_{i-1}|\sim\sqrt{D}\log\frac{\xi_{\sigma}}{\epsilon D},\quad i=2,\ldots,k.
Remark 2.1.

The spike cluster is established by a balance between repelling spikes and attracting boundary point of local maximum curvature.

Theorem 2.2.

The kk-boundary spike cluster solution given in Theorem 2.1 is linearly stable if τ\tau is small enough.

Remark 2.2.

There are eigenvalues of two different orders: n−1n-1 eigenvalue related to repelling of neighbouring spikes are of order ϵ3​log⁡ξσϵ​D\epsilon^{3}\log\frac{\xi_{\sigma}}{\epsilon D}, and one eigenvalue stemming from the curvature of the boundary (corresponding to synchronous motion of all spikes) is of order ϵ3\epsilon^{3}.

This paper is organised as follows. In sections 3-5 we show existence of the spike cluster steady state by using Liapunov-Schmidt reduction. In section 3 we introduce an approximation to the spike cluster steady state. In section 4 we use the Liapunov-Schmidt method to reduce the problem to finite dimensions. In section 5 we solve this reduced problem. In sections 6-7 we study the stability of this spike cluster steady state. In section 6 we consider large eigenvalues. Finally, in section 7 we study small eigenvalues. In two appendices we show some technical results: in appendix A (section 8) we prove Proposition 4.1 and in appendix B (section 9) we compute the small eigenvalues.

4. Existence I: Reduction to finite dimensions

Let us start to prove Theorem 2.1.

The first step is choosing a good approximate solution which was done in (3.6). The second step is using the Liapunov-Schmidt method to reduce the problem to a finite dimensions which we do in this section. The last step is solving the reduced problem which will be done in Section 5.

6. Study of the large eigenvalues

We consider the stability of the steady-state (u,v)(u,v) constructed in Theorem 2.1.

In this section, we first study the large eigenvalues which satisfy λε→λ0≠0\lambda_{\varepsilon}\to\lambda_{0}\neq 0 as max⁡{σ,D}→0\max\{\sigma,D\}\to 0.

Linearizing the system around the equilibrium states (u,v)(u,v) obtained in Theorem 2.1, we obtain the following eigenvalue problem:

{Δ​ϕ−ϕ+2​uv​ϕ−u2v2​ψ=λ​ϕ,Δ​ψ−σ2​ψ+2​u​ϕ=τ​λ​σ2​ψ\left\{\begin{array}[]{l}\Delta\phi-\phi+\frac{2u}{v}\phi-\frac{u^{2}}{v^{2}}\psi=\lambda\phi,\\[5.69054pt] \Delta\psi-\sigma^{2}\psi+2u\phi=\tau\lambda\sigma^{2}\psi\end{array}\right. (6.1)

for (ϕ,ψ)∈HN2​(Ωε)×HN2​(Ωε)(\phi,\psi)\in H^{2}_{N}(\Omega_{\varepsilon})\times H^{2}_{N}(\Omega_{\varepsilon}).

In this section, since we study the large eigenvalues, we may assume that |λε|≥c>0|\lambda_{\varepsilon}|\geq c>0 for max⁡{σ,D}\max\{\sigma,D\} small enough. If Re​(λε)≤−c<0\mbox{Re}(\lambda_{\varepsilon})\leq-c<0, then λε\lambda_{\varepsilon} is a stable large eigenvalue, we are done. Therefore, we may assume that Re​(λε)≥−c\mbox{Re}(\lambda_{\varepsilon})\geq-c and for a subsequence max⁡{σ,D}→0\max\{\sigma,D\}\to 0, λε→λ0≠0\lambda_{\varepsilon}\to\lambda_{0}\neq 0. We shall derive the limiting eigenvalue problem which is given by a coupled system of NLEPs.

The second equation of (6.1) is equivalent to

Δ​ψ−σ2​(1+τ​λε)​ψ+2​u​ϕ=0.\Delta\psi-\sigma^{2}(1+\tau\lambda_{\varepsilon})\psi+2u\phi=0. (6.2)

where the cutoff function χϵ\chi_{\epsilon} has been defined in (3.13).

7. Study of the small eigenvalues

Now we study the eigenvalue problem (6.1) with respect to small eigenvalues. Namely, we assume that λε→0\lambda_{\varepsilon}\to 0 as max⁡{σ,D}→0\max\{\sigma,D\}\to 0. We will show that the small eigenvalues in leading order are related to the matrix ℳ⁡(𝐩0)\mathcal{M}({\bf p}^{0}) given in (7.3) which is computed from the Green’s function. Our main result in this section says that if λε→0\lambda_{\varepsilon}\to 0, then in leading order

λε∼ξσ​σ0,\lambda_{\varepsilon}\sim\xi_{\sigma}\sigma_{0}, (7.1)

where σ0\sigma_{0} is an eigenvalue of ℳ⁡(𝐩0)\mathcal{M}({\bf p}^{0}). We will show that all the eigenvalues of ℳ⁡(𝐩0)\mathcal{M}({\bf p}^{0}) have negative real part provided that the eigenvector is orthogonal to (1,1,…,1)T(1,1,...,1)^{T}.

However, for the eigenvector (1,1,…,1)T(1,1,...,1)^{T} the eigenvalue of ℳ⁡(𝐩0)\mathcal{M}({\bf p}^{0}) is zero, the leading order term in the eigenvalue expansion vanishes and the next order term is needed to prove stability. To establish it we have to compute the contribution from the boundary curvature. It follows that for a local maximum point of the boundary curvature this eigenvalue has negative real part. Whereas the Green’s function part is of order ϵ3​log⁡ξσϵ​D\epsilon^{3}\log\frac{\xi_{\sigma}}{\epsilon D}, the part from the boundary curvature is of order ϵ3\epsilon^{3}. Thus the small eigenvalues of (6.1) are all stable.

To compute the small eigenvalues, we need to expand the spike cluster solution to higher order. Then we expand the eigenfunction and compute the small eigenvalues. This will be done in Appendix B. The key estimates are given in Lemma 9.1.

We compute the small eigenvalues using Lemma 9.1. Comparing l.h.s and r.h.s, we obtain

−ν2​ξσ2​ℳ​(𝐩0)​𝐚ε​(1+o⁡(1))=λε​ξσ​𝐚ε​∫ℝ+2(∂w∂y1)2​𝑑y​(1+o⁡(1)),\displaystyle-\nu_{2}\xi_{\sigma}^{2}\mathcal{M}({\bf p}^{0}){\bf a}_{\varepsilon}(1+o(1))=\lambda_{\varepsilon}\xi_{\sigma}{\bf a}_{\varepsilon}\int_{{\mathbb{R}}^{2}_{+}}(\frac{\partial w}{\partial y_{1}})^{2}\,dy(1+o(1)), (7.2)

where ν2\nu_{2} has been defined in (5.10). Further, we have

ℳ⁡(𝐩0)=(mi​j​(𝐩0))i,j=1k,\displaystyle\mathcal{M}({\bf p}^{0})=(m_{ij}({\bf p}^{0}))_{i,j=1}^{k}, (7.3)

where

9. Appendix B: Computation of the small eigenvalues

In this appendix we will compute the small eigenvalues. First we expand the solution to a higher degree of accuracy than in Section 3. Then we expand the eigenfunctions and finally we calculate the small eigenvalues.

9.1. Further expansion of the solution

In this subsection, we further improve our expansion to the solutions derived in Section 3.

First we define

Our main idea is to start with a single boundary spike solution of the Gierer-Meinhardt system in a disk BRB_{R} of radius RR such that the curvature at the centres of the boundary spikes on the disk and the domain ∂Ω\partial\Omega agree. Further, the boundary spike solution in the disk is invariant under rotations of the solution which results in a zero eigenvalue. Then the small eigenvalue of the boundary spike solution in Ω\Omega can be computed by a perturbation analysis of the disk case.

The single boundary spike solution (u0,v0)(u_{0},v_{0}) in the ball BRB_{R} with maxBR⁡u0=u0​(0,R)\max_{B_{R}}{u_{0}}=u_{0}(0,R) in polar coordinates solves the following system:

=ψε⟂​(pl)​(∫Ωε23​ul3v3​∂v∂τ⁡(pl)+O⁡(ε4))\displaystyle=\psi_{\varepsilon}^{\perp}(p_{l})(\int_{\Omega_{\varepsilon}}\frac{2}{3}\frac{u_{l}^{3}}{v^{3}}\frac{\partial v}{\partial\tau(p_{l})}+O(\varepsilon^{4}))
=O⁡(ξσ3​σ2​(ε​Dξσ​log⁡ε​Dξσ)2)=o⁡(ξσ2​σ2​ε​Dξσ).\displaystyle=O(\xi_{\sigma}^{3}\sigma^{2}(\frac{\varepsilon D}{\xi_{\sigma}}\log\frac{\varepsilon D}{\xi_{\sigma}})^{2})=o(\xi_{\sigma}^{2}\sigma^{2}\frac{\varepsilon D}{\xi_{\sigma}}).

and

J9,l\displaystyle J_{9,l} =∫Ωεul2v2​∂ul∂τ⁡(pl)​(ψε⟂​(x)−ψε⟂​(pl))​𝑑x\displaystyle=\int_{\Omega_{\varepsilon}}\frac{u_{l}^{2}}{v^{2}}\frac{\partial u_{l}}{\partial\tau(p_{l})}(\psi_{\varepsilon}^{\perp}(x)-\psi_{\varepsilon}^{\perp}(p_{l}))\,dx
=O⁡(ξσ2​σ3​ε​Dξσ​log⁡ε​Dξσ)=o⁡(ξσ2​σ2​ε​Dξσ)\displaystyle=O(\xi_{\sigma}^{2}\sigma^{3}\frac{\varepsilon D}{\xi_{\sigma}}\log\frac{\varepsilon D}{\xi_{\sigma}})=o(\xi_{\sigma}^{2}\sigma^{2}\frac{\varepsilon D}{\xi_{\sigma}})

Thus we have

J2,l=o⁡(ξσ2​σ2​ε​Dξσ).J_{2,l}=o(\xi_{\sigma}^{2}\sigma^{2}\frac{\varepsilon D}{\xi_{\sigma}}). (9.32)

and (9.20) follows. Last we consider J3,lJ_{3,l},

=O⁡(ξσ2​σ​ε​Dξσ​log⁡ε​Dξσ​λε)=o⁡(ξσ​λε).\displaystyle=O(\xi_{\sigma}^{2}\sigma\frac{\varepsilon D}{\xi_{\sigma}}\log\frac{\varepsilon D}{\xi_{\sigma}}\lambda_{\varepsilon})=o(\xi_{\sigma}\lambda_{\varepsilon}).

Thus (9.21) follows.
